decks.domain: The basics: turning, passing, lane changes, backing, parking and communicating with other drivers

cards.front: What should you do before any turn?
cards.back: Before any turn, check your mirrors, your surroundings and your blind spot, stay in your lane, signal your turn and yield the right-of-way.
cards.memory_hook: Check, stay in lane, signal, yield

cards.front: Why are last-second changes of plan dangerous before a turn?
cards.back: Last-second changes of plan are unsafe and can cause a crash, so check mirrors and the traffic behind you before turning into a side road or driveway.

cards.front: What must you avoid during a turn, and why give trucks and buses room?
cards.back: Do not change lanes in the middle of a turn or cut across the center line, and leave extra room for trucks and buses, which may swing over the center line as they turn.
cards.memory_hook: No lane changes; trucks swing wide

cards.front: A bus swings over the center line as it turns. May you do the same?
cards.back: Large trucks and buses may swing across the center line while turning, but you must not cross it yourself, so give them extra room instead.

cards.front: How do you set up a left turn at an intersection?
cards.back: For a left turn, check that your path is clear, keep near the center line, watch for pedestrians crossing on the left, and wait about halfway into the intersection while leaving room for oncoming turners.
cards.memory_hook: Clear path, near center, wait halfway

cards.front: How should your wheels point while you wait to turn left, and why?
cards.back: While waiting to turn left, keep the steering wheel and wheels straight, because if you are hit from behind with the wheel turned left you will be pushed into oncoming traffic.

decks.domain: The basics: turning, passing, lane changes, backing, parking and communicating with other drivers

cards.front: What is a U-turn, and is it always safe?
cards.back: A U-turn is one smooth U-shaped motion that reverses your direction, and it can be very dangerous even though some intersections allow it.
cards.memory_hook: One smooth motion; can be dangerous

cards.front: What should you check before making a U-turn?
cards.back: Before a U-turn, check all mirrors and traffic and look for any sign that prohibits it.

cards.front: When is a U-turn allowed on a rural two-lane highway?
cards.back: On any rural two-lane highway a U-turn is allowed as long as it is done safely and does not interfere with traffic.

cards.front: How is a U-turn made, and where is it allowed unless a sign forbids it?
cards.back: A U-turn is a single continuous motion and is allowed on any rural two-lane highway when safe, unless a sign forbids it.

cards.front: With multiple turn lanes, which lane should you finish the turn in?
cards.back: With multiple turn lanes, finish the turn in the matching lane: start in the left-most lane and end in the left-most lane, start in the middle and end in the middle.

cards.front: From which lane must you turn right on a four-lane roadway?
cards.back: When turning right from a four-lane roadway, the turn must be made from the lane closest to the right curb or road edge.
cards.memory_hook: Right turn from the curb lane

cards.front: Where should you use a Y-turn, and where else will you be asked to do one?
cards.back: Use a Y-turn only in residential areas on streets too narrow for a U-turn; you will also be asked to perform one on the driving exam.

cards.front: How does a Y-turn differ from a U-turn?
cards.back: A Y-turn is a stop-and-reverse turnaround reserved for residential streets too narrow for a U-turn, and it is also a graded maneuver on the driving exam.

cards.front: What is the first step of a Y-turn?
cards.back: Y-turn step one: signal right, check your mirrors and the traffic on your right, move over as far to the right as possible, and stop.

cards.front: What is the second step of a Y-turn?
cards.back: Y-turn step two is to signal left, check your blind spot, turn left across to the opposite curb and stop.

cards.front: What are the third and fourth steps of a Y-turn?
cards.back: Y-turn step three is to look back over your right shoulder and reverse just far enough to drive forward again, then stop; step four is to check left and right and pull forward into your lane.

cards.front: Which step of the Y-turn is the only one where you reverse?
cards.back: In the Y-turn the only reversing step is the third one, where you look back over your right shoulder before backing.

decks.domain: The basics: turning, passing, lane changes, backing, parking and communicating with other drivers

cards.front: When may you use a paved shoulder to get around a vehicle?
cards.back: You may use a paved shoulder to get around a vehicle only when that vehicle is stopped or is making a left turn.

cards.front: Which lane is for going around slower vehicles on a multi-lane road, and why is passing on the right risky?
cards.back: On a multi-lane road the left-most lane is the lane for going around slower vehicles, and passing on the right is risky because the other driver may not see you.
cards.memory_hook: Left lane passes; right is risky

cards.front: How does a normal pass differ from going around on the shoulder?
cards.back: Passing on the left is the normal pass, while going around on a paved shoulder is allowed only past a stopped or left-turning vehicle.

cards.front: What should you do when another driver is passing you?
cards.back: If another driver is trying to pass you, keep to your lane and slow down.

cards.front: What must you do before changing lanes?
cards.back: Before changing lanes, make sure the way is clear, signal first, move only one lane at a time, and look over the shoulder on the side you are moving toward.
cards.memory_hook: Clear, signal, one lane, shoulder check

cards.front: What are blind spots, and how do you check them?
cards.back: The areas you check over your left and right shoulders are blind spots, which cannot be seen by using your mirrors alone.

cards.front: Why are mirrors not enough before a lane change?
cards.back: Checking mirrors is not enough before a lane change, because the blind spots are seen only by looking over the shoulder toward the new lane.

cards.front: How many vehicles may you pass at once, and on which side?
cards.back: Pass only one vehicle at a time and only on the left, since there may not be time to get around several vehicles or even the one ahead of you.

cards.front: May you stay in the passing lane or speed up to finish a pass?
cards.back: Do not linger in the passing lane, and never exceed the speed limit to complete a pass.

cards.front: What room do you need before passing, and must others move over?
cards.back: Pass only when there is enough room in front of the vehicle you are passing, and remember that other drivers are not required to move over for you.

cards.front: Does passing change the speed limit or require the other driver to move over?
cards.back: The speed limit still applies while passing, and the vehicle being passed has no duty to move over for you.
cards.memory_hook: Limit stands; no duty to move

cards.front: When is it safe to return to the driving lane after passing?
cards.back: It is safe to return to the driving lane once both headlights of the vehicle you passed appear in your rearview mirror.

cards.front: What cue tells you it is safe to move back after passing?
cards.back: After passing, the cue that it is safe to move back into the driving lane is seeing both headlights of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.

decks.domain: The basics: turning, passing, lane changes, backing, parking and communicating with other drivers

cards.front: How far and how fast should you back up?
cards.back: Because it is hard to see behind a vehicle, back up as little as possible and no faster than a slow walk.

cards.front: How should you look when backing, besides mirrors and a camera?
cards.back: When backing, do not rely only on your mirrors and backup camera: turn your body, look over your right shoulder through the rear window, and use a helper outside the car when you can.
cards.memory_hook: Turn, look back, use a helper

cards.front: What should you do after backing, and what if you miss an exit?
cards.back: After backing, scan left and right before rejoining traffic, and if you miss an exit or turn, never back up; continue to the next exit and come back.

cards.front: You miss your highway exit. What do you do?
cards.back: A missed exit is handled by driving to the next exit and coming back, never by backing up on the road.

cards.front: Where should you normally park so your car is not a hazard?
cards.back: You are responsible for making sure your parked vehicle is not a hazard, which normally means parking on the far-right side, clear of any travel lane.

cards.front: Where is parking not allowed?
cards.back: Parking is not allowed along yellow-marked curbs, in front of fire hydrants, or where a No Parking sign is posted.

cards.front: How should you park on level ground?
cards.back: Park at a very low speed, and on level ground shift into Park, or into gear with a manual transmission, and set the parking brake.

cards.front: Which way do you turn the wheels when parked uphill with a curb?
cards.back: Parked uphill with a curb, turn the wheels all the way to the left before shifting into park.

cards.front: Which way do you turn the wheels when parked uphill without a curb?
cards.back: Parked uphill without a curb, turn the wheels all the way to the right before shifting into park.

cards.front: Which way do you turn the wheels when parked downhill, and what else do you set?
cards.back: Parked downhill, turn the wheels all the way to the right, and on any hill set the emergency brake.

cards.front: Which hill-parking case turns the wheels left, and which cases turn them right?
cards.back: Uphill with a curb is the left-wheel case, while uphill without a curb and every downhill park are right-wheel cases.

decks.domain: The basics: turning, passing, lane changes, backing, parking and communicating with other drivers

cards.front: What should you watch for, and how big a space do you need, to parallel park?
cards.back: For parallel parking between vehicles, watch for traffic, pedestrians and fixed objects, and look for a space about three-six feet longer than your vehicle.
cards.memory_hook: Space a bit longer than car

cards.front: How does parallel parking begin?
cards.back: Parallel parking starts with your turn signal on and a stop alongside the vehicle ahead of the space, about two feet away from it.

cards.front: How does the starting gap compare with the extra length of the space?
cards.back: When you begin parallel parking you stop about two feet from the car ahead, and the space you choose should be about three-six feet longer than your car.

cards.front: What is the next step after stopping beside the car ahead?
cards.back: Next, turn the wheel fully toward the side you are parking on, left for the left side of the road and right for the right side, and back up slowly.

cards.front: When do you straighten the wheel while backing into a parallel space?
cards.back: When your front door passes the rear bumper of the car you are parking behind, straighten the wheel and keep backing slowly in a straight line.

cards.front: When do you turn the wheel the other way while parallel parking?
cards.back: Once your bumper clears the vehicle in front, turn the wheel sharply the other way and back slowly until you are parallel to the curb.

cards.front: How do you finish a parallel park, and what distances should you end with?
cards.back: Finish by straightening the wheels, ending about a foot from the curb and at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind.

cards.front: How does the final curb distance compare with the distance from other vehicles?
cards.back: At the end of a parallel park you should be about a foot from the curb, but at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind.
cards.memory_hook: Close to curb, room between cars

cards.front: How do you let other drivers know where you are and what you plan?
cards.back: Let other drivers know where you are and what you intend by using headlights, brakes, turn signals and hazard lights, and by keeping space ahead and behind.

cards.front: Should you drive when you are very upset or excited?
cards.back: Strong emotions affect safe driving, so do not drive when you are very worried, excited, afraid, angry or depressed.

cards.front: What are a light tap and a hard press of the horn for?
cards.back: The horn exists to help prevent crashes: a light tap gets another driver's attention, and a hard press warns of a collision about to happen.

cards.front: How does a light horn tap differ from a hard press?
cards.back: A light tap on the horn is for getting attention, while a hard press is reserved for warning of an imminent collision.

cards.front: Why use low beams, and what should you know if they switch on automatically?
cards.back: Low beams help you see and be seen; even if your car switches them on automatically, learn the manual control and check that they come on when needed.

cards.front: When are low beams required?
cards.back: Low beams are required when you cannot see a vehicle or person five hundred feet away, about one block, and from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise.

cards.front: When are low beams recommended?
cards.back: Low beams are recommended whenever your windshield wipers are on and in rain, snow or fog.

cards.front: Which low-beam situations are required, and which are only recommended?
cards.back: Low beams are required at the five hundred-foot visibility threshold and in the half hour after sunset through the half hour before sunrise, but are only recommended with wipers on or in rain, snow or fog.

cards.front: When should you use high beams, and when must you dim them?
cards.back: High beams let you see twice as far as low beams; use them when no vehicles are approaching or in an unfamiliar place or construction area, and dim them for oncoming traffic.

cards.front: What should you do about an oncoming driver's high beams, and when are parking lights used?
cards.back: If an oncoming driver leaves the high beams on, look toward the right side of the road, and use parking lights only while parked and idling.

cards.front: How do high beams differ from parking lights in when they are used?
cards.back: High beams double your seeing distance compared with low beams, yet must be dimmed when a vehicle approaches; parking lights are only for when you are parked and idling.

decks.domain: The basics: turning, passing, lane changes, backing, parking and communicating with other drivers

cards.front: In what order do you signal and move, and how early do you signal before an intersection turn?
cards.back: Turn on your signal, check around you, and then move; at an intersection, begin signaling about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, before the turn.

cards.front: When your turn comes just after an intersection, when do you signal?
cards.back: When your turn comes just after an intersection, wait until you have crossed the intersection before signaling.

cards.front: How does signal timing differ for a turn at an intersection and a turn just past one?
cards.back: At an intersection you signal about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, ahead of the turn, but for a turn just past an intersection you wait until you have crossed it.

cards.front: When may hand signals replace turn signals, and what are the three signals?
cards.back: Hand signals may replace turn signals that are missing or hard to see: arm straight out the driver window to turn left, elbow bent with the hand up to turn right, and hand pointed down to slow or stop.
cards.memory_hook: Straight left, up right, down stop

cards.front: Which arm position means a left turn, a right turn, and slowing or stopping?
cards.back: In hand signals a straight arm means a left turn, an arm bent upward means a right turn, and an arm pointed down means slowing or stopping.

recap_hooks.text: Check mirrors and blind spot, stay in your lane, signal and yield before every turn.
Give trucks and buses room as they swing wide, but never cross the center line yourself.
Wait halfway into the intersection with your wheels straight before a left turn.
A U-turn is one smooth motion, allowed on rural two-lane highways when safe and not forbidden.
Finish multi-lane turns in the matching lane, and turn right from the curb lane.
A Y-turn is for narrow residential streets, and only its third step reverses.
Pass on the left, one vehicle at a time, and use the shoulder only around stopped or left-turning cars.
Check blind spots over your shoulder before a lane change.
Never speed to pass, and return when both headlights show in your mirror.
Back up little, slowly, looking over your shoulder.
Never back up for a missed exit.
Uphill with a curb, wheels left; every other hill, wheels right.
Choose a space a few feet longer than your car and start beside the car ahead.
Turn fully, straighten as your door passes the bumper, then turn the other way.
Finish about a foot from the curb with room ahead and behind.
Use lights, signals and space to show other drivers your plans, and drive calm.
Tap the horn for attention; press it hard to warn of a crash.
Low beams are required when your view is short and after dark, and recommended with wipers on.
Signal, check, then move, starting about three seconds before an intersection turn.
For a turn just past an intersection, cross first, then signal.
Hand signals: straight arm left, bent up right, pointed down to stop.
